title: What "Over 100 Applicants" on a LinkedIn Job Really Means (and Whether to Bother Applying)
summary: "Over 100 applicants" on LinkedIn counts apply clicks, not real applications, and it's capped. Here's why applying is usually still worth it, and what gets you seen.
body_text: What does "Over 100 applicants" on a LinkedIn job really mean? It mostly counts clicks on the Apply button, not finished, qualified, or screened applications. "Over 100" is also a display cap, so a role at 101 and a role at 4,000 look identical. Reposted jobs drag their old count along too. The real competition is far smaller than the label suggests, because recruiters filter to a short list of good-fit resumes and never read the whole pile. So applying is usually still worth it, as long as you fit and you're reasonably quick. You find a job you'd actually want. Good title, right level, salary in range. Then your eye catches the grey line under the button: Over 100 applicants . And something in your chest deflates. Why bother? A hundred people got there first, half of them probably better than you, and the thing's basically gone. Hold on. That number is not what you think it is, and the story you just told yourself about it is wrong in almost every part. The count is inflated, the label is capped, and the competition it implies is mostly imaginary. Below is what "Over 100 applicants" actually counts, why so much of it is noise, how small the real field usually is, and how to decide, quickly and without spiraling, whether a given posting is worth your time. What the number literally counts Start with the mechanics, because they change everything. On LinkedIn, that applicant count is, at its core, a tally of how many people clicked the Apply button. It doesn't measure how many submitted a finished application, whether any of them are qualified, or how many a recruiter has actually looked at. It measures clicks. This is easiest to see with the two kinds of apply buttons. When you see Easy Apply , you finish on LinkedIn, so LinkedIn does register that submission. But when you see the plain Apply button, LinkedIn hands you off to the company's own website or applicant tracking system to complete the application there. And here's the part almost nobody realizes: once you leave for that external site, LinkedIn loses sight of you. It doesn't get a record back of who finished. So it counts the click, because the click is the only thing it can see. LinkedIn's own advertising tools quietly admit the gap. In its Campaign Manager, "Job Apply Clicks" and "Job Applications" are two separate metrics, one for people who tapped Apply and one for people who actually submitted. The public-facing badge on a job post smooshes those two ideas into one word: applicants. On a posting that redirects out to a company ATS, that number can be a wild overstatement of who genuinely applied. Someone opens the job, clicks through to see what the company site wants, decides it's a fifteen-screen ordeal, and closes the tab. LinkedIn still logged one "applicant." "Over 100" is a cap, not a real count There's a second layer of fuzziness, and it's a design choice. LinkedIn stops showing you a real number once a posting crosses a threshold. The platform's maximum label is simply "Over 100 applicants." Past that point, everything reads the same. Think about what that hides. A posting sitting at exactly 101 apply-clicks looks identical to one that has pulled four thousand. You have no way to tell them apart from the badge. So the label you're reacting to isn't even a precise measure of the thing you're afraid of. It's a ceiling. For a remote, entry-level, or otherwise popular role, "Over 100" often means the true figure is somewhere in the hundreds or thousands, and for a niche or senior role it can mean the true figure is barely past a hundred, or lower once you strip out the click-and-bounce crowd. Same three words, completely different realities. Reposting muddies it further. When a company refreshes a listing, or LinkedIn bumps it on its automatic cadence, the post can show up looking new while still carrying the old applicant tally. Some setups even lump similar roles together, so an old account-manager posting with eighty clicks and a new one with eighty clicks can present as a hundred and sixty. You're not looking at a hundred and sixty fresh, eager competitors. You're looking at a running total that's been accumulating, sometimes for weeks, sometimes across more than one req. Why most of that pile is noise Now the quality question, which matters even more than the quantity one. The barrier to clicking Apply is close to zero. One button, a stored resume, done in four seconds. When something costs almost nothing to do, people do it constantly and carelessly. That's the whole reason the counts look the way they do. So who's actually in a pile of "Over 100"? A big chunk is spray-and-pray: folks firing the same resume at every posting in a category without reading the requirements. A chunk is geographically or legally impossible for that specific role, people who need sponsorship the company won't provide, or who are on the wrong continent for an in-office job. A chunk is agencies and staffing firms tossing candidates at anything open. And a large slice is simply not qualified, applying hopefully rather than seriously. This has gotten worse as tools that auto-submit applications on someone's behalf have flooded postings with volume that was never targeted in the first place; if you want the recruiter's-eye view of that flood, we covered whether AI auto-apply bots actually work and why volume was never the bottleneck. Recruiters see this every day, and they'll tell you the raw number and the number of real contenders are two different animals. A posting that shows three hundred "applicants" might contain a dozen people who genuinely match the must-haves. When a hiring team actually sorts a big pile, the first thing that happens is brutal subtraction: wrong location, no work authorization, missing a hard requirement stated plainly in the posting. Those get cut in seconds, often by the most junior person on the team, on a simple red-light-green-light pass. The scary headline number deflates fast the moment a human starts filtering it. Want recruiters to find you instead of scrolling past? Get a free LinkedIn review that checks your profile against what recruiters actually search for, so you show up in the sourcing they do in parallel with the applicant pile. Review My LinkedIn → The real competition is much smaller than the badge Here's the reframe that should take the sting out of the number. Nobody reads a hundred resumes and ranks you against all of them. That's not how the work gets done, and it's not physically possible when a popular posting can pull hundreds of clicks in a day. What recruiters usually do is sort the pile by date received and work from the top down, stopping once they've got a small handful of solid candidates to move forward. Ask a room of recruiters how they mechanically go through a list and most describe some version of the same routine: open the applicant tracking system, sort by most recent, start reading, and quit reading once they have enough good ones to fill the interview slots. That's often five to ten people. If your application is number two hundred and forty-seven in a stale pile, the honest truth is nobody may ever scroll that far. The other thing that shrinks the field is that hiring teams close reqs early. A recruiter drowning in a thousand resumes doesn't grind through all thousand. They pull the posting down, review what they've got, and either move forward or repost with tighter language. Plenty of them say the same thing out loud: once a role hits fifty or a hundred applicants, that's when you stop the intake and start reading, not at a thousand. The giant numbers you see are frequently postings that should already have been closed. Break down a single crowded role and the shape is familiar: three hundred-plus applications come in, about ten people with the relevant skills get called to interview, and two come out as real hire candidates. Treat those figures as one illustration rather than a universal ratio, but the shape holds everywhere. The pool collapses from "hundreds" to "the handful who clearly fit" almost immediately. You were never competing with three hundred people. You were competing with the ten who matched, and then with whoever landed near the top of the list. To see where this filtering sits inside the whole process, it helps to know how hiring actually works from posting to offer, because the applicant count lives at the very front of a long funnel that thins out fast. What actually decides whether you get seen If the number isn't your enemy, what is? Three things you can influence, and one you can build in the background. Take them in the order that moves your odds the most. Timing: apply while the pile is small Because recruiters work top-of-list and stop early, when you apply matters more than the count does. A good resume submitted in the first hours often beats a perfect one submitted on day four, purely because of where it lands in the queue. LinkedIn even flags this for you with a "Be an early applicant" note on fresh postings, which is worth acting on, though it's a nudge, not a guarantee. Set your filters to surface new roles fast and apply the same day, not over the weekend. On LinkedIn you can even tighten the "past 24 hours" filter by editing the search URL: the address contains &f_TPR=r86400 , which is 24 hours in seconds, and swapping in r14400 narrows it to the last four hours so you catch postings while the pile is still small. Speed only helps if you're ready to move, so having a strong resume queued up in advance is half the battle, which is the point of getting your job search set up to move quickly . Fit and keywords: survive the first cut The people doing the first cut aren't studying the nuance of your bullet points. They're scanning for a small set of signals that say "this person matches the title and the must-haves." So your resume needs to obviously mirror the role in the terms the posting and the tracking system use. You don't have to write a unique document from scratch for every single job, though. The saner move is to tailor to the job title or family, since most listings for the same role ask for broadly the same things, and then apply quickly across matching postings with that version. Keep it clean and readable so it parses; the whole "you have to trick the robot" fear is mostly overblown, which we unpack in the ATS auto-reject myth . If your applications keep vanishing, the reason is more often a genuine fit or clarity gap than the headline count, and why your resume keeps getting rejected walks through the fixable ones. Reach a human, not only the queue The single biggest way to skip the pile is to not be in the pile alone. A referral, a short note to someone on the team, a message to the hiring manager after you apply, any of these puts your name in front of a person instead of a queue. It doesn't have to be elaborate. A few sincere sentences about why you fit, sent to the right person, does more than a flawless application sitting at slot two hundred. Asking well is a skill in itself, and how to ask for a referral without making it awkward is worth getting right, because a referral quietly moves you out of the anonymous stack and to the top of someone's attention. Build a profile that gets you sourced in parallel While you're applying, recruiters for those same roles are often sourcing from the other direction, running searches and messaging people who fit, whether or not those people applied. A profile that clearly signals your title, skills, and level can pull inbound messages that bypass the applicant count completely. This channel isn't magic and it isn't evenly distributed, it tends to work better the more senior and specialized you are, but it's real, it runs alongside your applications, and it costs you nothing once the profile is set. That's the quiet argument for treating your LinkedIn as a live asset rather than a static resume dump. We get into why an optimized profile is the actual payoff in the ex-LinkedIn-insider myths , and it's also why a strong profile beats worrying about a number you can't control. When a high count actually is a reason to skip None of this means you should apply to everything with a giant number attached. It means the number alone shouldn't scare you off. There are real cases where a high count is a signal to spend your energy elsewhere, and the difference is triage, not fear. The clearest one: a posting that's been open for weeks, shows a huge count, and hasn't visibly moved. If a role has been sitting for a month with "Over 100" and keeps getting refreshed, you're often looking at a company hunting for a unicorn, a pipeline posting collecting resumes with no live opening, or a hiring process that's stalled. Applying there is a lower-odds bet than a fresh posting where you're a clean fit, and it's worth knowing what happens to applications that fall into that void, which is the whole subject of the job application black hole . When you're choosing where to spend a finite number of tailored applications, recency and fit should win over a role you'd be a marginal candidate for. But be careful with one specific inference: a reposted job is not automatically a rejection or a dead end. LinkedIn reposts on an automatic schedule, and companies often refresh listings on Mondays just to push them back up the feed. A repost can simply mean the role is still open, or that they're still screening, or that they want a rare skill they haven't found yet, which might be exactly your skill. If you interviewed somewhere and then saw the job reposted, don't read a rejection into it; teams keep sourcing in parallel and rarely bet on a single candidate. The rule of thumb: use a stale, sky-high count as a reason to deprioritize a posting you'd be a stretch for, not as a reason to abandon a fresh one you genuinely fit. The numbers you can't see cut both ways It's worth sitting with the fact that the count hides good news as often as bad. Because "Over 100" caps the display, you can't tell a lightly-contested role from a mobbed one. Because the number only reflects LinkedIn clicks, it says nothing about the people who found the job through the company site, an internal referral, or a recruiter's direct outreach. And because it counts clicks rather than finished applications, a meaningful share of any pile never actually completed the process. People land jobs off postings that showed enormous counts all the time, and usually find out the real number only after they've already got the offer. The person who almost didn't apply to a role because it read "Over 100," applied anyway, and got hired, is a genuinely common story. Had they trusted the badge, they'd have skipped the job that hired them. That's the whole risk of over-weighting a number designed more for at-a-glance impressions than for calculating your odds. A quick decision rule for any posting Here's a way to run the call in under a minute, so you stop re-litigating it every time you see a badge. First, do you actually fit the core must-haves? If yes, the count is close to irrelevant; apply. If you're a stretch, the count becomes a tiebreaker for where to spend limited effort. Second, how fresh is it? A posting from today or yesterday is worth applying to quickly regardless of the number, because you'll land near the top of the queue. A month-old posting with a huge count and repeated reposts, where you're only a partial fit, is a fair one to skip. Third, can you reach a human? If you can get a referral or message someone on the team, apply even to the crowded ones, because you're no longer competing on the anonymous pile. And fourth, is your profile set up so recruiters can find you independently? If not, that's the one fix that pays off across every application at once, so it's where a spare hour this week does the most good. Do those four checks and the applicant count shrinks back to what it actually is: one weak, capped, click-based signal among several stronger ones. It was never a measure of your odds, only a count of how many people tapped a button. Your odds come from fit, from timing, and from whether a real person ever lays eyes on your name. Don't let a vanity number talk you out of a job before the recruiter ever gets the chance to. Frequently Asked Questions Should I still apply if a job says "Over 100 applicants"? Usually, yes, if you genuinely fit the role. The badge counts apply-button clicks, not finished or qualified applications, and "Over 100" is a display cap that lumps a role at 101 in with one at 4,000. A recruiter is not ranking you against all hundred-plus. They're filtering to a short list of good-fit resumes and reading a fraction of the pile. The count is a weak signal. Your fit and how fast you apply matter far more. Does the applicant number mean 100 people actually completed applications? No. For postings with the plain Apply button, LinkedIn sends you to the company's own site to finish, then loses track of whether you did. It counts the click. Its own ad tools even keep "apply clicks" and "completed applications" as two separate numbers. So a chunk of any pile clicked through, saw a long form, and bailed. The public badge quietly treats all those clicks as "applicants." Why do some jobs hit 100+ applicants within an hour of posting? Two reasons, mostly. One, one-click applying is so frictionless that popular or remote roles pull huge volumes fast, much of it low-effort or unqualified. Two, the posting may not be brand new at all. Refreshed and reposted listings can appear fresh while carrying forward an applicant count that's been building for weeks, sometimes across more than one version of the role. A shockingly fast number is often an old number wearing a new timestamp. How many of those applicants are actually qualified? Fewer than the number suggests, though there's no single trustworthy percentage. A large share of any big pile is spray-and-pray applications, people in the wrong location, candidates needing sponsorship a company won't offer, or folks simply not matching the requirements. When a hiring team sorts a pile, those get cut in seconds. The genuinely competitive field is the smaller group who clearly meet the must-haves, which is who you're really up against. Do recruiters read every application? They don't, and they can't when a posting pulls hundreds. The common approach is to sort by date received, read from the top, and stop once there are enough strong candidates for the interview slots, often just five to ten. Reqs also get closed early, before the pile grows unmanageable. If your application sits deep in a stale list, it may never get opened, which is exactly why applying promptly beats applying perfectly-but-late. Is it worth applying to a reposted job? Often, yes. A repost doesn't reliably mean rejection. LinkedIn reposts on an automatic cadence, and companies frequently refresh listings just to bump them up the feed. A repost can mean the role is still open, they're still screening, or they want a rare skill nobody's brought yet. If you fit the requirements, go for it. The one to be wary of is a posting that's been open for weeks with a huge count and no visible movement, which is a weaker bet. How do I get seen when a posting already has a big pile? Apply fast, so you land near the top of the queue. Make your resume obviously match the role's title and keywords so you survive the first filter. And reach a human if you can, through a referral or a short note to someone on the team, which pulls your name out of the anonymous stack. Running quietly underneath all of that, a well-tuned profile lets recruiters find and message you directly, sidestepping the pile entirely. It also helps to understand what recruiters can and can't see on LinkedIn , so you present the right signals to the people doing that sourcing. Does applying early actually help? It genuinely can, because of how recruiters work. They tend to read from the most recent applications and stop when they've got enough good ones, so early arrivals get eyes that late arrivals may not. LinkedIn's "Be an early applicant" label points at this, and it's a nudge worth acting on rather than a hard promise. The practical move is to surface new roles quickly with tight filters and apply the same day instead of waiting for the weekend. Why does the number sometimes go down after I apply? Because it isn't a stable, tidy tally. Postings get refreshed, reposted, merged, or edited, and the displayed count can shift as a result. It's also capped and click-based rather than a precise measure of completed applications. Don't read meaning into small movements up or down. The number is a rough, at-a-glance impression, not an accurate scoreboard of the competition or of your standing in it. How do I stop the applicant count from psyching me out? Remember what it does and doesn't measure. It counts how many people tapped a button. It says nothing about your fit, your timing, or whether a human ever sees your name, which are the things that actually set your odds. People get hired off "Over 100" postings constantly and usually learn the real number only after the offer. Run a quick fit-and-freshness check, apply when you match, and don't let a capped vanity metric reject you before the recruiter does. title: Why we’re increasing the AI focus of our job board
summary: As a result of recent AI progress, we've decided to update our job board so that all roles aimed at experienced users relate to risk from transformative AI.
body_text: In light of AI progress this year, we have decided to stop posting senior-level and mid-career global health, animal welfare, and climate change roles on the 80,000 Hours job board. We will continue to post entry-level and junior roles, and we will link to other job boards that focus on these areas. Why we’re no longer posting mid- and senior-level roles in these areas AI progress this year (Claude Opus 4.5, 4.6, and 4.7, GPT-5.3-Codex, and Claude Mythos, all of which represented faster capability growth than I expected) has convinced me that the expected impact of work on transformative AI (TAI) has grown dramatically, relative to that of work on global health, animal welfare, or climate change (henceforth: non-TAI), and that we are entering an all-hands-on-deck situation for TAI. For the time being, our mission is best served by focusing on AI and roles related to catastrophic AI-mediated risks (e.g. biosecurity or AIxAnimals ). This is because: We have short timelines to transformative AI : We think it’s quite plausible that transformative AI will arrive in the next 5 years. While I used to be less confident in this, the progress since Opus 4.5 has made me think it is quite likely that by 2040 we will have reached transformative AI. Because we have so little time, transformative AI going well “ by default ” now seems relatively unlikely to me, which means there is a lot of work to be done. AI safety, biosecurity, and macrostrategy remain very neglected. Scenarios where AI capabilities ‘plateau’ now seem very unlikely. In such scenarios, the world would not change dramatically due to AI, and jobs in other areas would become relatively more important. But at this point, it seems like a mistake not to focus on worlds where the trends of the last few years continue. We aim to provide our users with the most promising roles for working on the world’s biggest problems. But in a world with imminent transformative AI, the most important intervention for human health and animal welfare is making sure that that transformation goes well. Thus, we’ve stopped recommending roles for experienced users on interventions that don’t engage with the coming changes. We believe their talent would, in expectation, go significantly further in roles focused on TAI. This is not a happy update for me. As I wrote during our strategic change in focus last year , I hate that this is the timeline we’re in. And while we could continue to post these roles because it’s what we’ve always done, because we don’t want to lose part of our audience, or because of an obligation to the EA community, we would rather act on our belief that we are entering an all-hands-on-deck situation. Why we’re still posting entry- and junior-level roles in non-TAI areas In addition to roles with high direct impact, we post roles where we believe people can build career capital to tackle the world’s most pressing problems. We believe that in certain early-career non-TAI opportunities, people can have impact on the world and build skills and habits of mind that would be hard to find elsewhere (For example, many global health and animal welfare charities in the EA space put a premium on calibration and expected-value thinking to an uncommon degree; both are very valuable in TAI work.) We’ll be making this more clear on the job board so people understand our views. In a way, we think about the primary value of these roles differently from the organisations that post them because we hope that people who take those roles will develop skills to later work on TAI. However, we believe this is better than us not posting these roles at all for the organisations. Why we’re still posting roles in other cause areas No changes are planned for our curation of roles in biosecurity, nuclear security, building effective altruism, or macrostrategy. We believe that these all have an important part to play as powerful AI enables bad actors, disrupts strategic stability, and creates new philosophical questions to grapple with. Also: Biosecurity continues to seem robustly good even without the complications of AIxBio. Macrostrategy and building effective altruism are important for continuing to probe the central questions of EA, including “Where can we do the most good?” Even though we’re committed to our current answer to that question, we think it must continue to be asked, so that we can update on future evidence and ideas. Some important arguments and questions that we’ve considered Non-TAI work remains much more tractable. This is fair, but we think this factor is not strong enough to overcome the increased urgency and importance of TAI roles. Fit matters; some people’s most impactful opportunities won’t involve TAI. A person’s fit for a role type usually doesn’t depend on its cause area. All areas need operations, strategy, communications, etc. Also, we’ve always had an impact ‘bar’ for roles, which means that some people’s personal best opportunities will be excluded. This is a concrete downside of having a bar, but the upside of having a bar is clarity for our audience about what we think the best options are. Won’t this shrink your audience, resulting in less attention to the cause areas you’re now prioritising? This is possible, but we think it’s an acceptable risk if it lets us act on our true beliefs. Additionally, our audience is already strongly AI-focused. Roughly 88% of our job board users since our first pivot last year have clicked either only or mostly TAI-relevant roles, 4% have clicked a balance, and 8% have clicked only or mostly non-TAI roles. We expect the AI-focused audience to grow alongside public interest in AI, and we don’t expect engagement to significantly decline with this change. Even if it did, that would not be a sufficient reason to continue posting roles that don’t seem as promising to us. Why bother posting non-TAI roles when you’ll have even fewer now? We continue to think that non-TAI entry- and junior-level roles are above our bar because of the career capital they provide. Additionally, this change hasn’t led to a dramatic drop in the number of non-TAI roles. While we’ve removed senior- and mid-career roles in these areas, we’ll be slightly expanding our criteria for early-career roles, which will somewhat make up for it. Will this put you out of sync with the rest of 80,000 Hours? The job board has been more pluralistic than the rest of 80,000 Hours since last year’s pivot . This change will put us more in line with our other programmes (such as advising), which are strongly TAI-focused. Other job boards We think there are reasonable perspectives within which non-TAI roles could be just as impactful as TAI-relevant roles (e.g. Marcus Davis’s arguments for epistemic humility ). In other words, we could be wrong. Thus, we are happy to recommend other job boards which focus more on these roles, and now feature links to these job boards more prominently on our own, so that people who come to us looking for non-TAI roles can still find what they’re looking for. These job boards are: The EA Opportunity Board . The Opportunity Board is focused more specifically on EA organisations than we are. Animal Advocacy Careers . They do great work in sharing animal welfare roles. Probably Good . We appreciate their breadth of coverage of roles. We have been coordinating with these other job boards to ensure they can continue supporting organisations we’ve supported in the past. Appreciation I know that this is unwelcome news for some in our audience and for many organisations that we’ve supported for years, and I’m sorry. We are making our best guess about the greatest dangers of the next decade. It is my dear hope that we are wrong. I made this decision as 80,000 Hours’ job board manager, but my strong appreciation goes out to many of my colleagues for their contributions to and debate on this decision, particularly Huon, Arden, Jess, Bella, Jenna, and Alice. Thanks also go out to Dylan and Thane at Probably Good, Agnes at CEA, and Ana at AAC for their spirit of collaboration. Thanks are also due to Nina Friedrich, Zach Robinson, and Gergő Gáspár for their thoughts. Like (opens in new window) Post (opens in new window) Share (opens in new window) Email Print

title: Introducing web-scale /monitor: Always-on search across the entire web
summary: Firecrawl /monitor now watches the entire web, pinging you or your agent the moment something relevant comes online.
body_text: Today we're launching web-scale /monitor : an always-on search that watches the web and pings you or your agent the moment something comes online. Before, /monitor only worked for single pages or websites. You named the URLs, Firecrawl diffed them on a schedule, and notified you when something changed. Now you can use that same power on the entire web. Define a query and a goal, and Firecrawl runs the search on your schedule, dedupes results, and alerts only when new, relevant pages appear. Every run delivers what's new and meaningful to your AI agent or app, via webhook or email. What is web-scale /monitor? Web-scale /monitor finds new pages across the web as they appear. You define one or more search queries, a recency window, and a plain-language goal. On every check, Firecrawl: Runs the queries against the web Filters to results inside your searchWindow Dedupes by canonical URL against prior checks Judges new results against your goal (when judging is enabled) Pings you or your agent when something worth acting on comes online Pages and sites vs. the entire web Page/Site Monitoring Web Monitoring Scope Single pages or websites you name The entire web You provide URLs or a site to crawl Search queries + a goal Each check Scrapes known pages and diffs them Searches the web for new matches Alerts on Content changes on watched URLs New results the judge finds relevant Best for Pricing pages, changelogs, docs you already track Regulations, competitor moves, breaking stories Same scheduling, goals, judging, and notification channels underneath. If you've used /monitor for page watching, the API shape will feel familiar: web monitors use a search target instead of URLs. Create your first web monitor A web monitor is a standard create_monitor call with a type: "search" target: from firecrawl import Firecrawl firecrawl = Firecrawl (api_key = "fc-YOUR-API-KEY" ) monitor = firecrawl . create_monitor ( name = "AI coding assistant launches" , schedule = { "text" : "every 30 minutes" , "timezone" : "UTC" }, goal = "Alert when a new open-source AI coding assistant is announced. Ignore funding rounds and unrelated AI news." , targets = [ { "type" : "search" , "queries" : [ "open source AI coding assistant launch" ], "searchWindow" : "24h" , "maxResults" : 10 , } ], notification = { "email" : { "enabled" : True , "recipients" : [ "alerts@example.com" ], "includeDiffs" : True , } }, ) print (monitor.id) The same call in Node: import Firecrawl from "@mendable/firecrawl-js" ; const firecrawl = new Firecrawl ({ apiKey : "fc-YOUR-API-KEY" }); const monitor = await firecrawl .createMonitor ({ name : "AI coding assistant launches" , schedule : { text : "every 30 minutes" , timezone : "UTC" } , goal : "Alert when a new open-source AI coding assistant is announced. Ignore funding rounds and unrelated AI news." , targets : [ { type : "search" , queries : [ "open source AI coding assistant launch" ] , searchWindow : "24h" , maxResults : 10 , } , ] , notification : { email : { enabled : true , recipients : [ "alerts@example.com" ] , includeDiffs : true , } , } , }); console .log ( monitor .id); Tune recall and precision Two levers do different jobs: queries control recall: what each search pulls in. Cast a wide enough net with relevant terms and variations, then let your goal decide what actually alerts. goal controls precision: which retrieved results actually alert. Good queries read like search terms, not sentences. Use includeDomains and excludeDomains for domain scoping instead of site: operators in the query string: { "type" : "search" , "queries" : [ "FDA drug approval" , "clinical trial results" ] , "searchWindow" : "24h" , "maxResults" : 10 , "includeDomains" : [ "fda.gov" , "clinicaltrials.gov" ] } Get pinged by webhook or email Point a webhook at your agent and subscribe to monitor.page and monitor.check.completed , the same events page monitors use. When a new matching result comes online, the payload arrives with status: "new" and a judgment explaining why it matters: { "success" : true , "type" : "monitor.page" , "data" : [ { "monitorId" : "019df960-06e7-7383-9d89-82c0113dc31a" , "checkId" : "019df960-5f2a-75fb-a98b-bd2d32ca67d4" , "url" : "https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=40000000" , "status" : "new" , "isMeaningful" : true , "judgment" : { "meaningful" : true , "confidence" : "high" , "reason" : "A new open-source AI coding assistant was announced, which matches the monitor goal." } } ] } Email summaries work the same way: sent only when a check surfaces new or errored results. What you can build with web-scale /monitor Use case Example queries Goal Track regulatory and legal changes FDA approval , clinical trial posting , SEC filing Alert when a new approval, trial, or filing is published Monitor competitor developments "Acme Corp" funding OR acquisition , competitor careers site Alert on funding rounds, new roles, or product launches Track breaking news and events Phase 3 trial results biotech , M&A filing Alert when trial results or deal filings appear Replace the DIY stack Before web-scale /monitor , staying current on the open web meant wiring together a scheduler, a search API, deduplication logic, a relevance filter, and a notification layer, then maintaining all of it as queries and sources shift. One endpoint replaces that stack. You define the query once; Firecrawl handles the always-on search, dedupe, classification, and delivery. Pricing: web monitors cost 2 credits per 10 results per check, plus 1 credit per result the judge evaluates when judging is enabled. There is no separate per-monitor fee. Try it today Web-scale /monitor is live for all Firecrawl users. title: Who Groutes the Base Plates? Division 03 Scope Conflicts GCs Miss at Bid
summary: Grouting base plates falls between concrete and steel scopes on almost every project. See the Division 03 conflict that creates $100K+ change orders.
body_text: TL;DR Base plate grouting is one of the most common Division 03 / Division 05 scope conflicts in commercial construction. Neither the concrete sub nor the steel sub explicitly owns it in most bid packages — and neither prices it unless told to. If your scope sheets don't assign it, you absorb it or fight over it at closeout. The fix is upstream: drawings-first scoping, explicit trade assignments, and a pre-issue scope review before bid day. This conflict appears in Chapter 5 of the Scope Gap Playbook alongside a dozen other trade-specific gaps that show up across commercial GC bids. The Question Nobody Answers at Bid Structural steel is going up. The iron workers have bolted the first columns. The concrete sub has finished the slab pour. Then someone asks: "Who's grouting the base plates?" Silence. This is not a rare situation. It plays out on commercial, institutional, and industrial projects across North America — every year. The concrete sub says it's structural steel work. The steel sub says it's concrete finishing. The GC is stuck in the middle with a field crew waiting and a change order forming. The problem started at bid, not in the field. And it started because nobody wrote it down. Why Base Plate Grouting Is a Structural Gap, Not an Afterthought Grouting base plates is load-bearing work. It transfers column loads to foundations. It's not a finish — it's structural. If it's done wrong or late, it affects the entire steel erection sequence. The material is typically non-shrink cementitious grout. The work requires tight tolerance, proper curing, and coordination with the steel erector's schedule. It is not something a concrete crew can just swing back to do between pours. Structurally, this work belongs to the concrete scope. Sequentially, it belongs to the steel erection schedule. That tension is exactly why it falls through the cracks. What the Specs Say (and Don't Say) Most project specs reference base plate grouting in Division 03 (Concrete) under section 03 60 00 (Grouting) or 03 62 00 (Non-Shrink Grouting). Some specs reference it in Division 05 under structural steel installation notes. Here is the problem: specs often describe the product and the method. They rarely assign the trade. When a spec says "Contractor shall install non-shrink grout at all base plates per manufacturer's instructions," it uses "Contractor" — not "concrete subcontractor" or "steel erector." In a design-bid-build delivery model, "Contractor" means the GC. The GC then needs to assign that scope to a sub. If the GC doesn't explicitly do that in the scope sheet, nobody prices it. How the Conflict Unfolds on a Real Project Here is a typical sequence. It's not hypothetical — it's pulled directly from patterns documented across 200+ GC interviews conducted for the Scope Gap Playbook . Bid phase: GC sends bid docs to the concrete sub and the steel sub. Neither scope sheet explicitly assigns base plate grouting. Both subs exclude it — sometimes explicitly, sometimes silently. Buyout phase: GC reviews leveling sheets. Grout line items aren't there. No one flags it because both subs' numbers look competitive. Construction phase: Steel erection starts. Base plates are set. The steel sub requests grouting so they can continue erection. The concrete sub says it wasn't in their scope. Change order phase: GC absorbs the cost or negotiates a split. The fight usually runs $30K to $150K depending on project size and grout volume. This is a textbook scope gap. It was predictable. It was preventable. The "As Per Plans and Specs" Problem The most common anti-pattern in GC scope sheets — documented repeatedly in the Scope Gap Playbook — is the phrase "as per plans and specs." It sounds complete. It isn't. "As per plans and specs" doesn't assign a trade. It doesn't tell a concrete sub that base plate grouting is their scope. It tells them to read 2,000 pages and figure it out. Most subs read what they know and price what they see. If they've never owned base plate grouting before, they won't price it. A Pre-Construction Lead at a Top-ENR Canadian GC put it plainly: "It's descriptive — bread, put it on a plate, use the open jar. You have to get to that level of detail or else they'll just be like, 'you didn't tell us that.'" That's the peanut-butter test. If your scope sheet doesn't spell out that the concrete sub is responsible for non-shrink grouting at all structural base plates per Section 03 62 00, you have not been descriptive enough. Division 03 Scope Conflicts Beyond Base Plates Base plate grouting is one of several concrete-related scope gaps that show up regularly across commercial bids. The pattern is consistent: the spec describes the work, nobody assigns the trade, and the GC absorbs it at closeout. Slab Assembly Conflicts On projects with composite steel decks, conflicts arise between the steel sub and the concrete sub over who places the shear studs, who installs the edge form, and who is responsible for concrete mix placement above deck. Each sub assumes the other is pricing it. Concrete Pumping Pumping is frequently excluded from concrete sub bids. Some subs price direct chute or buggy placement. When the building height or pour location requires a pump, the GC either pays for it separately or finds it missing at buyout. If your scope sheet doesn't say "pumping included," assume it isn't. Grouting Embed Plates and Anchor Bolts Structural embeds set in concrete and anchor bolt chases are another grey zone. The steel sub installs the embed. The concrete sub pours around it. Who groutes the void? Same conflict, smaller dollar value — but it adds up across a full structure. The Scope Gap Playbook's trade-specific chapter covers these concrete conflicts alongside steel, MEP, envelope, and specialty trade gaps that cost GCs real money at closeout. What It Actually Costs The dollar value of a single base plate grouting gap depends on the project size, the number of columns, and the grout volume. On a mid-size commercial structure with 80 columns, the grout cost alone can run $40K to $100K. Add mobilization for a concrete crew, coordination delays, and any rework from late grouting affecting the erection schedule — and the total exposure climbs fast. Scope gaps like this compound. According to Arcadis's 2025 Global Construction Disputes Report, the average U.S. construction dispute in 2026 is worth $60.1 million. "Errors and omissions in contract documents" has been the top dispute cause for six of the past nine years. Base plate grouting conflicts fit that category exactly. FMI's Construction Disconnected report puts annual U.S. rework costs at $31 billion. Twenty-six percent of that rework traces back to communication breakdowns — and scope gaps that weren't resolved at bid are a primary driver. These are not abstract numbers. They show up in your margin on every project where scope isn't nailed down at bid. The Five Habits That Prevent This Gap The firms with the tightest margins on concrete-heavy work share a set of scoping habits. These align directly with the Eight Habits framework from the Scope Gap Playbook . 1. Drawings-First, Not Boilerplate-First Pull the structural drawings before you touch last project's scope template. Look at the base plate schedule. Count the columns. Note the grout specification. Then write the concrete sub's scope to match what's on this project — not what was on the last one. 2. Specific Document References Instead of "all concrete work as per plans and specs," write "non-shrink grouting at all structural base plates per Section 03 62 00, including all locations shown on Structural Drawings S-series, columns and base plates as noted on the Base Plate Schedule." That is not bureaucratic over-engineering. That is protection. 3. Front-Load the Buyout Conversation Flag base plate grouting at the leveling meeting. Ask the concrete sub directly: "Have you included non-shrink grout at base plates?" Get a written confirmation. If they excluded it, get a price before award — not after the steel erector is standing around waiting. 4. Sub-Specific Tailoring An Estimating Manager at a Canadian ICI GC noted that subs have become more likely to call out scope exclusions explicitly: "We have less subs who just kind of a gentleman's agreement — they've become more quick to clarify that we're not including that one piece of scope." That shift works in your favor only if your scope sheet gives them something specific to respond to. 5. The Pre-Issue Scope Review Before you send the scope to the sub, have someone review it against the structural drawings. Not a five-minute skim — a real check against the spec sections and the structural engineer's notes. If your team is covering too many pursuits to do this consistently, that is a workflow problem worth solving at the process level. Where AI Fits in Catching Division 03 Conflicts Reviewing 2,000 pages of specs and a full structural drawing set for trade assignment conflicts is time-consuming work. Most estimating teams are carrying too many bids to do it thoroughly on every pursuit. Provision's Scope Agent reads the full project set — drawings, specs, and contracts — and generates a complete scope-of-work package in under 60 minutes. It flags exactly the kind of trade-assignment gaps described in this article: where the spec references a scope item but no trade has been assigned, where Division 03 and Division 05 cross-reference each other without a clear owner, and where grouting or embed work is described but not allocated. It's not replacing an experienced estimator's judgment. It's making sure your estimator isn't missing items at 11 PM on bid day because the grouting note was buried in a structural drawing note block on sheet S-04. Provision has processed over 66,000 construction documents and reviewed more than $100 billion in project value. On pre-built risk checklists, the platform delivers 99.5% accuracy. That's the level of review your concrete scope sheets need — but rarely get. If you want to see how it handles a Division 03 scope package, book a demo and bring a real project set. How to Write the Concrete Scope Sheet for Base Plate Grouting Here is a working example. This is what explicit scope language looks like for this item. Scope Item Vague Version (Anti-Pattern) Explicit Version (Best Practice) Base Plate Grouting All concrete work as per plans and specs Supply and install non-shrink cementitious grout at all structural base plates per Section 03 62 00. Includes all columns shown on Base Plate Schedule, Drawings S-101 to S-108. Coordinate schedule with steel erector. Embed Plates Per structural drawings Dry-pack grouting at all structural embed plate voids following steel installation. Includes locations noted on Structural Drawings and Structural Notes. Concrete Pumping Concrete placement as required Concrete pumping included for all elevated pours and locations where direct chute or buggy placement is not feasible. Pump setup and washout included. This level of specificity takes an extra 20 minutes per trade scope. It saves days of dispute resolution. The Broader Pattern: Division 03 Is Not a Simple Trade Concrete work touches almost every other trade on a commercial project. It touches civil at the site boundary. It touches steel at every base plate and embed. It touches MEP at every sleeve and blockout. It touches envelope at grade beams and foundation waterproofing. Every one of those interfaces is a potential scope gap. The GC who wins on concrete-heavy projects is the one who maps those interfaces at bid — not after award. A Director of Pre-Construction at a Mid-Market Southeast GC described the internal version of this problem: "Pre-con is working in the scope sheet world and project management is working in the scopes of work." When those two documents aren't aligned, the field team inherits the gap. And they price it as a change order. The Scope Gap Playbook's trade-specific chapter maps the most common Division 03, 05, and MEP conflicts with the same level of specificity as this article. If your team is building or revising concrete scope templates in 2026, it's worth reading alongside this post. Bottom Line Base plate grouting lands in no-man's land because it sits at the intersection of Division 03 and Division 05. Specs describe it. Drawings show it. Scope sheets ignore it. And subs price what their scope sheet tells them to price. The solution is not complicated. It requires looking at the drawings, reading the spec sections, and writing scope language specific enough that a sub has no excuse to exclude it. That work happens at bid — or it happens as a change order at closeout. Your margin doesn't have room for the second option. Frequently Asked Questions What is base plate grouting in construction? Base plate grouting is the installation of non-shrink cementitious grout beneath structural steel column base plates. It fills the gap between the base plate and the foundation to ensure full, uniform bearing and proper load transfer. It's structural work — not a finish — and it directly affects column stability and the steel erection sequence. Who is responsible for grouting base plates — the concrete sub or the steel sub? There is no universal rule. Most project specs place base plate grouting in Division 03, which points to the concrete subcontractor. But the work is coordinated with the steel erection schedule, which creates ambiguity. The GC must explicitly assign the trade in the scope sheet. If it isn't assigned, neither sub prices it. Why do Division 03 scope gaps happen so often? Division 03 work touches nearly every other trade — civil, steel, MEP, envelope. Each interface is a potential gap. Most scope sheets are built from templates, not from a drawings-first review. When nobody reads the structural notes against the Division 03 spec sections, items like base plate grouting fall through. The anti-pattern is generic scope language like "as per plans and specs" with no trade assignment. What does a base plate grouting scope conflict cost on a real project? On a mid-size commercial structure with 80 columns, the direct grout cost can run $40K to $100K. Add crew mobilization, coordination delays, and any schedule impact on steel erection, and total exposure often exceeds $100K. Arcadis reports the average U.S. construction dispute is now worth $60.1 million — and scope omissions are the top driver. How do I prevent this gap in my concrete scope sheets? Start with the drawings, not the template. Reference the specific spec section (typically 03 62 00) and the drawing sheets where base plates appear. Assign the trade explicitly. Confirm at the buyout leveling meeting that the sub has priced it. Then do a pre-issue scope review before the package goes out. These five steps take under an hour and eliminate the gap entirely. title: What is an Event Agenda? Examples and Guide
summary: The agenda for an event can vary depending on the type of event and the specific goals of the organizers but is is very important.
body_text: Marketing Posted on July 1, 2026 Picture this scenario: You wake up at 6 a.m. to catch an early flight to a nearby city for an industry event that starts at 10 a.m. You arrive by 9:30 a.m., so you wait in the main hall for the meeting to start. However, by 10:30 a.m., the meeting has yet to begin because many speakers have yet to arrive. The meeting eventually starts at 11:45 a.m. when people start complaining. Halfway through the event, the moderator announces that a critical event session won’t occur because the speaker canceled last minute. At the end of the meeting, you head home two hours late, disappointed because the session you most looked forward to didn’t happen. This scenario, unfortunately, isn’t rare—it usually happens when there’s no agenda to keep track of all the moving parts of an event. Read on to find out what an event agenda is, why you need one, how to write an event agenda, and some examples of event agendas to inspire your own. Table of Contents Toggle What is an event agenda? An event agenda is a breakdown of everything that’ll happen during an event and the amount of time allocated to each activity or session. This gives your organizers, attendees, and speakers a bird’s-eye view of the event and allows them to decide which presentations, sessions, and networking opportunities they most want to participate in. This breakdown may include the following: Company name Title of the event Date and location of the event Mission and objectives Moderators Guest speakers, if any Knowledge sessions, including the keynote speech, seminars, and webinars Networking opportunities, including 1-on-1 networking sessions, cocktail parties, and gala dinners Workshops, if any Breaks Social activities, such as board games, quizzes, interactive Q&As, and more Entertainment, including singers/bands, stand-up comedy, and magic shows Instructions on what to do should any aspect of the event go wrong Whether planning an in-person, virtual, or hybrid event , an event agenda ensures that your event runs correctly and your audience’s expectations align. When to create an event agenda You should create your event agenda early in the event planning process —before inviting guests to your event, renting a building, opening the web portal for registrations, and promoting your event. Once you invite your guests, you can send out the event agenda, invitation, and reminder emails . This gives your guests enough time to decide which sessions they’ll attend and come up with any questions they want answered. Why should you create an event agenda? An event agenda is like a master list of every activity during your event. It’s a roadmap that keeps everything on track. Without it, your event runs the risk of going off the rails. Here are three reasons you should create an event agenda: Agenda objectives can attract your target audience. Nobody wants to be absent from an industry-focused event where thought leaders break down relevant strategies that brought them success. Or an event where you can announce a breakthrough scientific discovery. In your event agenda, you get a chance to outline your objectives and let people know your event’s main attraction(s). These objectives define who’ll attend and who won’t. If you want the top people in your industry or stakeholders with shared goals to attend, your agenda’s objectives can draw them in. Event agendas help you manage time better. Events can be bustling, especially if hundreds of people are attending. Your event may become rowdy as sessions overlap if you don’t manage time well. An event agenda specifies how long each session will take, clearing up any confusion about where each speaker should be and how long they should speak. Event agendas give attendees and speakers time to prepare Your event agenda lets attendees and speakers know where they’re going and how long they can expect to spend there. This gives speakers time to create engaging speeches. It also gives attendees time to clear up their schedules, make arrangements for their families for the day (if they have one), and prep questions for the speakers at the event. How to write an event agenda Event agendas are necessary because they clarify what will happen at the event when there are breaks and when the audience will ask questions. To create an event agenda, here are the steps to take: 1.Know your goal for the event. What results do you want your event attendees to achieve? Do you want them to gain more industry knowledge? Network with other professionals? Build brand recognition. Knowing the goal for your event early on in the planning process can give you an idea of what activities the event will comprise, the kinds of speakers you’ll invite, and the budget you need to pull the whole thing off. For example, if you want attendees to leave with more knowledge than they came with, you’ll include specialized classes and workshops in the event schedule. But if networking is the goal, there’ll be breakout sessions and ice-breaker activities to help attendees interact with one another. Pro tip: Have a meeting with your company’s event team and important decision-makers to figure out what the goal is for the event. 2.Research guest speakers Having guest speakers at your event ensures that attendees get access to more knowledge and information about their industry. So once you know what your event goal is, discuss it with your team and get a list of dream speakers, industry experts, and niche workshop teachers. When your speaker list is ready, start contacting them and asking them to speak at your event. If possible, offer them something in return as an incentive—preferably monetary payment. Pro tip: Make a spreadsheet organizing all your potential speakers and use tags to label them— contract signed, undecided, no contract. This makes it easier to see which speakers are on hold, which ones need a reminder, and which ones you should strike out. 3.Ask attendees for their input. To appropriately tailor your event to your audience, ask your audience what they want to see at your event. You can do this by sending surveys or conducting in-person interviews. Even though your event already has a theme, asking your guests for their input can help you personalize the event to an extent. It also tells them that you value their opinions. Here are some questions you can ask: Which topics (or speakers) would you like to see at this event? What are you hoping to learn at this event? What are your goals for this event? What are you most likely to do between sessions? Pro tip: At the end of the event, send a post-event survey asking attendees what parts of the event were most valuable and which parts could use some improvements. This will give you an idea of how to make future events better. 4.Set a “free” date for the event. When setting dates for events, there’s a lot to look out for. First, you have to make sure that the date is one that your company’s key decision-makers and speakers agree on. You also need to ensure no prominent local events, such as football (or other sports) games, music festivals, and even scheduled constructions in the area may disrupt your circumstances. These events cause traffic jams and an influx of metro passengers that can delay your attendees. 5.Tailor event duration to your target audience Before setting your event’s start and end times, think about your target audience. Some people prefer to leave home early for an event, while others prefer staying out at night. The goal is to set times suitable for early birds and night owls. Pro tip: Use the staggered hour system, which allows attendees to vary their start and end times to suit their work and personal commitments. 6.Organize your sessions Depending on your event’s size and format, organizing your sessions by topics can be helpful. This makes it easier for your attendees to find the sessions they’re interested in without being overwhelmed. Talk to each of your speakers and moderator about what topic or session they’ll cover—from the keynote presentation to seminars to networking opportunities. Pro tip: Try to cram only a few sessions into tiny windows. If you do, your attendees may experience decision fatigue and gain little from the event. 7.Add times to each session. As you create your event agenda, include how long each session will take—including times for breaks and meals if they’re part of the event. This makes it easy for attendees to plan their time well. Try to give your speakers as much time as reasonably possible for each session so that no session infringes on another. Pro tip: Giving your speakers and moderators a 5- or 10-minute warning to signal the end of a session will help them wrap up any ongoing conversations before the next session starts. 8.Hold Q&A sessions After a session, it’s normal—expected, even—for attendees to have questions they want answered. Q&A sessions allow them to ask speakers their questions and get some answers. Not only do these sessions increase your audience’s new knowledge, but it also encourages interactivity between attendees and speakers—which is central to the success of any event. After the event, commemorative custom gifts can be given to attendees. Gifts don’t have to be expensive, but a well-chosen souvenir can not only deepen the emotional bond between attendees but also showcase the organizer’s unique taste and enhance attendees’ meeting experience. For example, Custom Pens can not only show the cultural taste of the organizer and have unique commemorative significance but also play practical value for participants in their daily work, allowing participants to feel the organizer’s intentions while enjoying a good time. Pro tip: Apart from networking sessions, you can encourage interactivity in other fun ways by playing games, hosting quizzes, and doing karaoke shows. Examples of Event Agenda If you’re looking for event agendas to inspire your own, here are three free templates you can use: Corporate event agenda template Suppose you’re hosting corporate events, such as summits, product launches, or award ceremonies. In that case, this event agenda template can help you specify the order of events, speakers that’ll take charge of each speech/session, and the time each session will take. 2. Networking event agenda template If you’re planning a networking or matchmaking event, this agenda template helps you specify the date, time, and location of the event, as well as each activity and how long it’ll go on. 3. Event planning agenda template Planning an event also needs an agenda to track how well the preparations are coming along. This template allows you to list, in sequential order, the steps you need to take to set up a great event. Notice how the template has fields where you can specify your target audience, event objectives, and risk assessment. This helps you stay on track so that your event generates the best results for your company. Keep track of event activities with an event agenda A good event agenda can boost the experience of both event planners and attendees alike. Since event agendas outline every activity and the times they’ll happen, attendees will find it easy to navigate the event. And you’ll have what you need to ensure that everything works smoothly. If you’re planning to host an event or conference, event management software like InEvent can make things easier for you. With solutions for in-personal, virtual, and hybrid events, InEvent helps you build stunning landing pages and websites so you can promote your event. This tool also provides you with a professional studio with state-of-the-art technology so you can create stunning broadcasts. For virtual events, InEvent helps your attendees interact with speakers through questions, built-in chat, and polls. And you can host smooth-sailing hybrid events with InEvent’s custom event app and omnichannel messaging system that eases communication between live and virtual attendees and speakers. title: June Updates
summary: Monthly updates featuring the latest added features, improvements, and bug fixes.
body_text: ​ New Features ​ Card Brand Details The Card Brands endpoint now returns a structured details object on each brand, giving you the full marketing-level terms behind a user’s card, including APRs, fees, rewards, and promotional offers. APRs : Purchase and cash-advance APR ranges via purchase_apr_min / purchase_apr_max and cash_advance_apr_min / cash_advance_apr_max . Fees : annual_fee and late_payment_fee . Rewards : A full rewards object with program name, reward type (for example, cash_back , points , miles ), and per-category earn rates (dining, travel, groceries, gas, and more), including the base-rate category for all other purchases. Promotions : A promotions array covering sign-up bonuses, intro APR offers, statement credits, and more, each with value, spend requirement, qualifying period, and expiration. Classification and freshness : card_category classifies the card (for example, travel , cash_back , store ), and data_as_of tells you when the details were last captured. Key Use Cases Power balance-transfer and refinance offers with accurate rate and promotion data. Enrich PFM experiences by showing users the detailed terms and benefits of the cards they carry. Optimize checkout and reward experiences by auto-routing purchases to the top-earning card. Card Brands is available as both a Product (on-demand) and a Subscription (near real-time updates), and the details object is available on API version 2025-07-04 and later. The endpoint is available to partners processing payments through the Payment Instruments endpoint. Contact your Method CSM to enable it. See the Card Brands reference to get started. ​ Dashboard: Check Payment Management Admins can now manage check payments directly from the payment detail page in the Method Dashboard . Stop payment : Place a stop on a paper check that has been sent but not yet cashed. The check is stopped and funds are reversed to the source. Check endorsement image : View the front and back endorsed image of a check once it has been cashed. Source & destination status : The payment detail page now surfaces source status and destination status alongside the existing payment status for better visibility into where a payment is in its lifecycle. Stop payment and check image viewing are available to admin users only. For more information, visit the Method Dashboard . ​ Preauth Signals The new Preauth Signals endpoint returns the predicted likelihood that a transaction will succeed, alongside verified ownership of the card and recommended retry timing. Built for merchants and commerce platforms looking to optimize payment performance. Key Use Cases Predict whether a card payment will go through before attempting the charge to reduce false declines at checkout. Identify the best date to retry a payment for recurring charges. This endpoint is currently in Public Preview. Reach out to your Method CSM for access and documentation. ​ New Attributes: Delinquency, HELOC & Available Credit New entity-level and account-level attributes give you a more complete, real-time picture of borrower risk and capacity. Delinquency signals : Aggregate borrower-level risk with the worst days-past-due bucket across accounts, whether delinquency is progressing or recently cured, total delinquent balance, and the highest-severity outcome (charge-off, collections, foreclosure, and more). HELOC-specific attributes : You can now separate out attributes related to HELOCs from mortgages and personal loans to isolate appetite for a new HELOC, CLI, or refi. Available credit : Understand a borrower’s total credit headroom in near real time to assess their riskiness and eligibility for new products. Direct Pay enrichment : Completed attribute responses now include Method Direct Pay history (recency, amount, and trailing 12-month count), providing a clearer picture of a borrower’s risk profile and appetite for debt consolidation. For more information, visit the Entity Attributes and Account Attributes API documentation. ​ Account Attribute Subscriptions Method now triggers events whenever an account’s attributes change, so you can react to balance, utilization, and delinquency shifts in real time instead of polling. Subscribe to the attributes you care about and Method delivers updates to your configured webhooks as they occur. Manage what you listen to through the Subscriptions endpoint . Receive changes through Events and webhooks. This pairs naturally with continuous, post-origination portfolio monitoring use cases. ​ Team IP Allowlisting Teams can now restrict API access to a defined set of IP addresses. Once an allowlist is configured, requests from outside the approved ranges are rejected, with enforcement backed by a 24-hour cache for low-latency checks. See IP Whitelisting to configure. ​ Improvements ​ Payments More accurate estimated completion dates : The estimated_completion_date returned on a payment now always shows the correct date or a slightly conservative estimate, especially for same-day ACH source payments. Destination posted date : The destination_posted_date field is now populated once the destination posts, giving you a precise reconciliation signal that is distinct from the estimated completion date. For more information, visit the Payments API documentation. ​ Payment Limits To protect platform safety and stability, per-transaction and 24-hour limits are now enforced on payment volumes. A new Limits tab under Dashboard Settings surfaces your team’s money-movement capabilities and associated limits in one place. You can now see at a glance what your team is permitted to send and receive, and where caps apply. Contact your customer success manager to learn more about your team’s limits.
